Quantum Channel Attention for ASL Alphabet Classification

Quantum Channel Attention for ASL Alphabet Classification

Final report with unfrozen signer-held-out validation

1. Project Overview

This project evaluates variational quantum circuits as channel-attention mechanisms inside pretrained convolutional image classifiers for American Sign Language (ASL) recognition. The central question is not whether a hybrid model can fit the dataset, but whether a quantum channel-attention (QCA) block offers better parameter efficiency or low-data generalisation than fair classical alternatives.

The study uses the Kaggle ASL Alphabet dataset: 87,000 RGB images across 29 classes (A–Z, del, nothing, and space). A fixed stratified split seed of 42 produces 69,600 training, 8,700 validation, and 8,700 test images. Low-data experiments subsample only the training split and leave validation and test unchanged.

One example from each of the 29 source-dataset classes. The shared capture background helps explain why random image-level splitting is unusually easy.

The principal result is negative: under matched frozen conditions, QCA does not outperform Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE), and a parameter-matched classical MLP outperforms QCA at 10% training data. In a separate unfrozen signer-held-out study, QCA’s small pooled lead is not significant and disappears under equal-signer averaging. The work demonstrates a functioning hybrid implementation, but it does not demonstrate a quantum advantage.

2. Architecture

2.1 Phase 0 — DenseNet121 Baseline

The baseline model is a standard pretrained DenseNet121 fine-tuned end-to-end on the ASL dataset. It serves as the accuracy ceiling reference.

Input Image (224×224×3)
    ↓
DenseNet121 Feature Extractor     [pretrained ImageNet weights, all params trainable]
    ↓
Global Average Pooling            → (B, 1024)
    ↓
Linear(1024 → 29)                 [classification head]
    ↓
Output Logits (29 classes)

Trainable parameters: 6,983,581

2.2 Phase 2 — DenseNet121 + Quantum Channel Attention

The hybrid model replaces the direct pooled-features-to-classifier path with a Quantum Channel Attention (QCA) block inserted between the pooled feature vector and the final classifier. This is inspired by the Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) network architecture, but the gating function is implemented as a variational quantum circuit instead of classical fully-connected layers.

Input Image (224×224×3)
    ↓
DenseNet121 Feature Extractor     [pretrained ImageNet weights]
    ↓
Global Average Pooling            → (B, 1024)
    ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               Quantum Channel Attention Block                │
│                                                             │
│  Linear(1024 → 8)          [classical down-projection]      │
│  tanh(·) × π/2             [angle encoding rescaling]       │
│  AngleEmbedding (8 qubits) [classical → quantum state]      │
│  StronglyEntanglingLayers  [2 variational layers, 8 qubits] │
│  ⟨Z⟩ measurement × 8      [quantum → classical, ∈ [-1,1]]  │
│  Linear(8 → 1024)          [classical up-projection]        │
│  Sigmoid                   [attention weights ∈ (0,1)]      │
│  x × attention             [feature reweighting]            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    ↓
Linear(1024 → 29)                 [classification head]
    ↓
Output Logits (29 classes)

Quantum attention parameters: 17,464
Total trainable parameters (frozen backbone): 47,189
Total trainable parameters (unfrozen backbone): 7,001,045

The quantum circuit uses PennyLane with the default.qubit simulator, AngleEmbedding for data encoding, and StronglyEntanglingLayers as the variational ansatz. Gradients are computed via backpropagation through the quantum circuit (diff_method="backprop").

2.3 Matched classical controls

All controlled comparisons freeze the same pretrained DenseNet121 backbone. The trainable alternatives after global pooling are:

  • No attention: classifier only; 0 attention and 29,725 trainable parameters.
  • SE: two-layer squeeze-and-excitation gate; 131,072 attention and 160,797 trainable parameters.
  • Matched MLP: an 8-dimensional nonlinear bottleneck with 17,480 attention and 47,205 trainable parameters, only 16 more than QCA.
  • QCA-v1: 17,464 attention and 47,189 trainable parameters.

The matched MLP is the most important control because it isolates the quantum circuit from the effects of adding a similarly sized nonlinear attention block.

2.4 QCA-v2 data re-uploading

QCA-v2 re-embeds the projected inputs before each variational layer while keeping the same 17,464 parameters. It was evaluated as a targeted 1%, single-seed pilot. This was an architecture probe, not part of the confirmatory three-seed comparison.

3. Experimental Setup

Setting Value
Software Python 3.12.11, PyTorch 2.12.0, PennyLane 0.45.0
Hardware Apple M4 Air; MPS for CNN operations, CPU for quantum simulation
Split Stratified 80/10/10, fixed split seed 42
Low-data seeds 42, 43, 44; training subset only
Optimiser / schedule AdamW / cosine annealing
Controlled runs 15 epochs, LR 1e-3, batch size 32, frozen backbone
External signer folds 15 epochs, backbone LR 1e-5, head LR 1e-3, batch size 32, fully unfrozen
Image size 224×224
Data augmentation Random rotation ±10°, colour jitter (no horizontal flip — ASL signs are handedness-sensitive)
Primary metrics Held-out test accuracy and macro-F1

Every reported low-data checkpoint was evaluated independently with src.evaluate; the three-seed summaries use sample standard deviation. Parameter counts come from reconstructed model parameters, not file size.

The matched frozen comparison is the informative one. SE exceeds QCA by 1.12 percentage points. QCA exceeds no attention by only 0.09 points in this single-seed full-data run. The unfrozen results only demonstrate saturation; they cannot identify an attention-module contribution.

SE ranks first at all three fractions. QCA trails no attention by 2.53 points at 1% and 0.30 points at 5%; at 10% it leads no attention by only 0.17 points, which is smaller than the across-seed variation. The parameter-matched MLP beats QCA by 0.58 points at 10%.

4.7 QCA-v2 data re-uploading pilot

At 1% training data and seed 42, QCA-v2 achieved 61.38% test accuracy and 0.6007 macro-F1, compared with 61.83% and 0.6030 for matched QCA-v1. Re-uploading reduced accuracy by 0.45 points while retaining the same 17,464 parameters. One seed is not sufficient for a general claim, but this pilot provides no rationale for a larger QCA-v2 sweep.

4.8 Unfrozen signer-held-out evaluation

Following supervisory guidance, a second study fine-tuned every DenseNet layer rather than freezing the backbone. It used the A–Z subset of MU HandImages: 1,815 images from five signers. For each fold, one signer was reserved for testing and 15% of the remaining-signers’ images formed a stratified validation set. All models trained for 15 epochs with backbone LR 1e-5, head LR 1e-3, batch size 32, and seed 42.

The public mirror is strongly signer-imbalanced: signers 1–5 contribute 650, 645, 130, 130, and 260 A–Z images. Equal-signer means are therefore the primary summary; pooled metrics are included but overweight signers 1 and 2.

Method Attention Params Trainable Params Signer Accuracy (mean ± SD) Signer Macro-F1 (mean ± SD) Pooled Accuracy Pooled Macro-F1
No attention 0 6,980,506 94.78% ± 5.17% 0.9461 ± 0.0528 94.82% 0.9477
SE 131,072 7,111,578 93.72% ± 5.17% 0.9304 ± 0.0543 94.71% 0.9463
Matched MLP 17,480 6,997,986 94.55% ± 4.02% 0.9395 ± 0.0445 94.88% 0.9482
QCA-v1 17,464 6,997,970 94.50% ± 4.95% 0.9426 ± 0.0494 94.99% 0.9497

QCA has the highest pooled accuracy by 0.11 points over the matched MLP, but not the highest equal-signer mean. Its paired signer-level accuracy differences are not significant versus no attention (p=0.543), SE (p=0.116), or the matched MLP (p=0.943; paired two-sided t-tests, five folds). Exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests reach the same conclusion (p=0.75, 0.25, and 1.00). This study therefore provides no statistically supported quantum advantage.

5. Key Findings

  1. No quantum advantage was observed. QCA never ranks first under the matched frozen-backbone conditions, and no paired external comparison is statistically significant.
  2. SE is strongest only in the frozen study. It leads at 1%, 5%, 10%, and full training data there, but not in the unfrozen signer-held-out study.
  3. QCA is smaller than SE, but less accurate. It uses 7.5× fewer attention parameters, with a 1.12-point full-data accuracy deficit. This is a size–accuracy trade-off, not evidence of quantum superiority.
  4. QCA does not reliably improve over omitting attention. Its differences from no attention range from −2.53 to +0.17 points in the low-data study.
  5. The matched MLP removes parameter count as an explanation. It exceeds QCA at 10%, and the two methods are close at 5%; QCA only leads at 1%, while both trail no attention and SE.
  6. Data re-uploading did not improve the pilot. QCA-v2 was 0.45 points worse than QCA-v1 for the matched 1%-seed-42 condition.
  7. Perfect unfrozen scores are not evidence for the attention head. The plain DenseNet121 baseline also achieves 100%, showing that the split is saturated under full fine-tuning.
  8. External signer-held-out results are effectively tied. QCA has the highest pooled accuracy (94.99%), while no attention has the highest equal-signer mean (94.78%); QCA’s advantages and deficits are all statistically inconclusive across five signers.

6. Limitations and Threats to Validity

  • Image-level random split: the Kaggle dataset does not expose signer IDs for a signer-disjoint split. Correlated background, capture conditions, or near-duplicate samples may occur across train, validation, and test sets.
  • Repeated use of one held-out split: all model families are ultimately compared on the same 8,700-image test partition. This supports controlled comparison but does not establish external generalisation.
  • Simulation only: the quantum layer runs on an ideal state-vector simulator. The study makes no claim about execution time, energy, or performance on quantum hardware.
  • Restricted architecture search: QCA-v1 was fixed at eight qubits and two layers. QCA-v2 was a one-seed pilot. Broader tuning after observing test results would increase selection bias and is not justified by the current evidence.
  • Three low-data seeds: these quantify training-subset variation, but confidence intervals remain broad and the image split itself is fixed.
  • Accuracy is near saturation: the full-data split is too easy to distinguish strong unfrozen models.
  • External signer imbalance: MU signer sample counts range from 130 to
    1. Pooled metrics are dominated by the two largest signers, while five signer-level observations provide low statistical power.
  • One external training seed: all five external folds use seed 42. Signer variation is measured, but stochastic training variation is not.
  • Validation is not signer-held-out: validation images are stratified from the four non-test signers. Test signers remain completely unseen during training and checkpoint selection.
  • Dataset provenance: the original MU hosting page is unavailable. The experiment uses a public mirror of the published filename-encoded dataset; this mirror does not declare a separate licence.

7. Conclusion

This study establishes a reproducible hybrid DenseNet–QCA pipeline and a controlled comparison against no attention, SE, and a parameter-matched MLP. QCA is parameter-efficient relative to SE, but that efficiency comes with lower accuracy in the frozen study. Across the tested low-data conditions, SE is consistently best, and QCA does not show a reliable advantage over either no attention or the matched classical MLP. QCA-v2 data re-uploading also fails to improve its matched pilot. In the unfrozen signer-held-out study, all four methods are close: QCA leads the pooled metric by 0.11 points, but trails the no-attention and matched-MLP equal-signer means, with no significant paired difference.

The scientifically supported conclusion is therefore negative: the experiments do not demonstrate that quantum channel attention is superior to classical CNN or ANN alternatives. Both the original controlled study and the unfrozen external signer-held-out extension are complete. Additional architecture or seed sweeps should be motivated prospectively rather than used to search for a favorable post-hoc result.

9. Protocol Amendment and Data Provenance

The initial external protocol proposed zero-shot evaluation of the frozen 10%-data checkpoints. Before any MU model result was examined, supervisory guidance rejected frozen backbones as the main study. The protocol was amended to full end-to-end fine-tuning with identical differential learning rates for all four methods. Signer 1 was used first to verify runtime; no model, hyperparameter, or stopping-rule change was made before running signers 2–5.

The experiment uses the A–Z subset of MU HandImages ASL (Barczak et al.). The original description and filename metadata are available from the Massey University repository. Because the legacy download is unavailable, images were obtained from the public mirror at hajarek24/asl-sign-language-recognition, revision 1e23d649fab0fbb1d4cac523d0c93b1ab06e2213. The mirror contains 2,515 images across 36 alphanumeric classes, of which 1,815 A–Z images were used.
